head:
Health · Weight and fitness

Being thin is not being fit

You step on a scale and it gives you a number. You take a fitness test and it gives you another. People often assume the second is just a finer version of the first. Studies following hundreds of thousands of adults say otherwise: at the same weight, fitness separates very different trajectories, and a low weight guarantees neither good fitness nor good health.

The problem

Take two 35-year-olds, an imaginary example to set out the problem. Camille weighs 58 kg, eats little and hardly ever moves. Thomas weighs 98 kg and has been training four times a week for years. On a scale, Camille looks “better”. On an endurance or strength test, the gap would very probably go the other way. Which of the two is more likely to be in good health in twenty years?

Many people answer Camille without hesitation, because thinness serves as a shortcut for health throughout sport and public health culture. Is that shortcut justified? This is the question every test on this site asks without saying so: they weigh nothing. They measure what your body can do, at a given speed, load and duration. If weight and fitness were the same thing, these tests would teach you nothing your scale does not already know.

The question

Do weight and fitness measure the same thing? When your scale goes down, does your fitness go up, and when your scale reads low, are you fit?

What is at stake

This is not a quarrel between experts. Depending on what you believe, you do not make the same choices, and those choices have concrete consequences.

Your health. If weight is your only dashboard, a thin, sedentary person gets a falsely reassuring signal. Conversely, a heavier person who trains regularly gets a permanent signal of failure, even though their body may be doing exactly what it should. In both cases, the number does not say what you think it says.

Your method. If the goal is a weight, you can reach it by eating less and moving little. That builds no capacity, and the review by Gaesser and Angadi (2021) reports that repeated weight changes are associated with muscle loss.14 If the goal is performance, the path goes through training, which changes the body from the inside, whether or not the scale moves.

Your independence and lifespan. Muscle and endurance determine what you can do at 40, 60 or 80: carrying, climbing, running after a bus, getting back up. In a study of more than 3,600 older adults, the quarter with the most muscle mass had lower mortality than the quarter with the least.12 What the scale lumps together in a single number therefore has parts that do not weigh equally on your future.

It would be dishonest to answer “weight does not matter”. We will see that it does. But the question remains open: does it matter for the same reason, in the same place, as fitness? Until that is answered, you may be following the wrong number.
rest:
The demonstration

Step 1 of 6

Weight is a single number, and it does not say what it is made of

Weight relative to height gives the body mass index (BMI): your weight divided by your height squared. By construction, it adds everything up: fat, muscle, bone, water. Two people can have the same BMI with a very different composition. The first question is therefore a practical one: when someone has too much fat mass, does BMI detect it?

A meta-analysis compiled 25 articles, 32 samples and 31,968 patients, comparing common BMI cut-offs with fat mass measured by a reference technique.10 Two notions to keep in mind. Sensitivity is the share of people with excess fat that BMI picks up. Specificity is the share of people without excess that it rightly rules out. Result: sensitivity of 0.50 (interval of 0.43 to 0.57) and specificity of 0.90 for the common cut-offs; for the cut-off of 30, sensitivity of 0.42 and specificity of 0.97.

BMI picks up half of the cases of excess fat, no more

Pooled values from a meta-analysis of 25 articles, shown per 100 people (0.50 becomes 50, and so on). Results vary a lot from one study to another, so these are orders of magnitude. Source: Okorodudu et al., International Journal of Obesity, 2010.10

What this means

When BMI says “excess”, it is rarely wrong: it rightly rules out 97 people out of 100 for the cut-off of 30. When it says “no excess”, it lets a large share of true cases through: the authors conclude that it misses half of the people who have too much fat mass. For the cut-off of 30, that is 58 out of 100 (derived calculation: 100 minus 42). A reassuring weight is therefore not proof of good body composition.

This does not yet tell us whether this “hidden” fat has consequences. That is the next step.

Step 2 of 6

A normal weight can hide a body at risk, and muscle matters

Researchers at the Mayo Clinic isolated, in the US survey NHANES III, 6,171 adults over 20 whose BMI was normal (18.5 to 24.9). They split them into thirds according to their percentage of fat mass. The top third (over 23.1% in men, over 33.3% in women) received the label “normal-weight obesity”; it is also described as “thin on the outside, fat on the inside”. Median follow-up was 8.8 years.11

At the same weight, metabolic syndrome is far more common when fat mass is high

Prevalence of metabolic syndrome by fat mass in normal-weight adults. 6,171 adults, NHANES III. The “3.5 times” ratio is calculated from the two percentages. Source: Romero-Corral et al., European Heart Journal, 2010.11

What this means

Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of several abnormalities (blood pressure, blood glucose, blood fats, waist circumference) that often precedes diabetes and heart disease. At the same weight, it is about 3.5 times more common in the group with the highest fat mass (16.6% versus 4.8%). The number on the scale does not tell these two groups apart.

Among the women in this group, the risk of dying from cardiovascular disease is multiplied by 2.2 after adjustment, with a wide interval (1.03 to 4.67), so a fragile estimate. A letter from readers published after the article points out that the study finds no association in men, nor with total mortality in either sex, and that the adjustment for BMI is open to question.11 The metabolic signal is solid; the mortality signal much less so.

The other half of composition is lean mass, of which muscle makes up most. Also in NHANES III, 3,659 older adults (men aged 55 and over, women aged 65 and over) were classified according to their muscle mass index, the amount of muscle relative to height, measured by bioimpedance. The quarter with the most muscle had lower mortality than the quarter with the least. The authors stress that this is an association, not proof of cause, and that the measurement method is not the most precise.12

What this means

Two bodies of the same weight do not have the same split between fat and muscle, and that split predicts different risks. Muscle is not an aesthetic detail: it is part of what predicts survival in older adults. Weight, for its part, adds the two together without telling them apart.

Body composition matters, but it is hard to see without a device. There is a measure that captures its effects through what the body can do: fitness. This is what we now set against weight.

Step 3 of 6

At the same weight, it is fitness that separates the trajectories

A meta-analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2025 pooled 20 cohorts, or 398,716 observations, of adults followed for 7.7 to 26 years. In each study, the “fit” group is the one with the best cardiorespiratory fitness, and the “low fitness” group the one with the lowest. Each is cross-tabulated with weight category (normal, overweight, obesity). The reference group is “normal weight, fit”.1

At the same weight, people with low fitness have about twice the risk

Risk ratio for all-cause death (95% confidence interval) compared with the normal-weight, fit group. 20 cohorts, 398,716 observations. Source: meta-analysis, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025.1,2

What this means

A ratio of 1 means the same risk as the reference group; 1.92 means 92% more. The three fit groups, whatever their weight, cannot be detectably distinguished from the reference group. The three low-fitness groups have a risk 1.8 to 2 times higher, including people of normal weight. Being thin and having low fitness therefore does not protect: in these data, it is fitness, not weight, that separates the two packs.

Caution is needed on one point. For people with obesity who are fit, the ratio is 1.11 with an interval of 0.88 to 1.40: no difference is detected, but the interval does not rule out an excess risk of around 40%. For comparison with another group, the risk of fit people with obesity (1.11) is about 58% of that of normal-weight people with low fitness (1.92), a derived calculation that points the same way as the formula reported in the press, according to which their risk is close to half.2

This result is not isolated. An older cohort of 21,925 men tested on a treadmill, with 428 deaths on average 8 years later, had found that thin men with low fitness had a risk of death about double that of thin fit men (relative risk of 2.07, interval of 1.16 to 3.69), and higher than that of fit men with obesity. Even more telling: men with low fitness and a waist circumference under 87 cm had a higher risk of death than fit men whose waist circumference exceeded 99 cm. The authors conclude that the benefits of thinness are limited to fit men.5 An earlier meta-analysis of 10 articles, published in 2014 by Barry and colleagues, pointed the same way: people with low fitness had about twice the risk whatever their BMI, and fit people with overweight or obesity had a risk close to that of fit people of normal weight.3,4

Finally, among 122,007 patients tested on a treadmill at the Cleveland Clinic, the risk of death fell at each fitness level, with a ratio of 5.04 between the lowest level and the elite, in calculations that take into account, among other things, weight, age, smoking and diabetes.15 The link with fitness is therefore not explained simply by the fact that fit people are thinner.

What this means

Three independent cohorts, different methods, the same direction. The question “am I thin?” and the question “am I fit?” have independent answers, and it is the second that is most closely linked to the risk of death. Camille, our example, cannot take reassurance from weight alone.

This does not mean weight is unimportant. The next step looks at what remains when we look at weight in its own right.

Step 4 of 6

What fitness does not erase: weight still matters

The Global BMI Mortality Collaboration pooled 10,625,411 people from 239 prospective studies. The main analysis covers nearly 4 million non-smokers with no chronic disease at baseline, who survived 5 years, with a median follow-up of 13.7 years for the whole sample. This precaution limits the bias whereby people who are already ill lose weight and die.9

Risk rises with obesity, and also below 18.5

Risk ratio for all-cause death by BMI band, compared with the band of 22.5 to under 25. Non-smokers with no chronic disease, 5-year survivors. This analysis does not take fitness into account. Source: Global BMI Mortality Collaboration, The Lancet, 2016.9

What this means

The curve is J-shaped. Risk climbs clearly with obesity: 1.45 for 30 to 35, 1.94 for 35 to 40, 2.76 beyond 40. It is also higher below 18.5 (1.51). And within the so-called normal range, being at 20 rather than 24 makes no difference (1.00 in both bands). Extreme thinness is not health, and obesity remains an established risk factor. This figure says nothing about fitness, which was not measured.

It remains to be seen whether fitness cancels this risk or only reduces it. For cardiovascular mortality, the 2025 meta-analysis gives a more nuanced picture.1

For the heart, the excess in fit people is not ruled out, but it is uncertain

Risk ratio for cardiovascular death (95% interval) compared with the normal-weight, fit group. Same meta-analysis as in step 3. Source: British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025.1

What this means

People with low fitness remain at 2 to 3.4 times the reference risk. For fit people with overweight (1.50) or obesity (1.62), the intervals include 1: we cannot say there is an excess, but we cannot rule it out, and the central value remains above 1. The authors specify that the estimate for people with obesity and low fitness is not robust: it becomes non-significant if a single study or the largest cohort is removed. A 2021 review reports, for the same cardiovascular mortality, a risk of 1.25 and 1.42 in fit people with overweight and obesity in another meta-analysis (Barry, 2018).4

Other work points the same way. A meta-analysis of eight studies (61,386 people, 3,988 deaths or cardiovascular events) distinguishes “metabolically healthy” people with obesity from the others. Overall, their risk is close to that of normal-weight people in good metabolic health. But keeping only the studies with at least 10 years of follow-up, they have a higher risk (ratio of 1.24). And people who are metabolically unwell are at risk whatever their weight: a normal-weight person with a poor metabolic profile has the same risk as a person with overweight or obesity and an identical profile.8

The study by Ortega and colleagues, on 43,265 people from the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study, illustrates the optimistic side. 46% of the people with obesity were metabolically healthy, and they had a 38% lower risk of death than those who were metabolically unwell, with no significant difference from normal-weight people in good metabolic health. This group was fitter than most people with obesity. Commentators are not fooled: a Yale physician (David Katz) points out that you can be heavy and fit, but that relatively few people are, and the British Heart Foundation maintains that obesity is an undeniable risk factor for most people.7 Another study, of 25,714 men, observed that about half of the men with obesity had low cardiorespiratory fitness, and that this low fitness predicted mortality in all BMI groups.6

What this means

Two statements are true at the same time. Fitness greatly reduces the gap in risk linked to weight, and it is the variable that best separates the groups. But it does not necessarily erase all of the risk of obesity, especially in the long term and for the heart. The message is not “weight does not matter”. It is “weight alone is not enough, and fitness cannot be read from the scale”.

If fitness weighs this much, we need to ask whether it can be worked on independently of weight, and whether working on it changes anything.

Step 5 of 6

Fitness can change, even when weight does not move

A study of 14,345 men who had at least two complete examinations followed changes in fitness and BMI over six years, then mortality over more than eleven years. Each additional MET of capacity (the MET is the unit of exercise capacity measured on a treadmill) was associated with a 15% lower risk of all-cause death, and 19% for cardiovascular deaths. Losing fitness was associated with a higher risk, whatever the change in BMI. The change in BMI, weight or fat mass was not associated with the risk of death.13

What this means

In this cohort, what mattered for survival was not whether the men lost or gained weight over six years, but whether they gained or lost capacity. About 90% of them were of normal weight or overweight at baseline: the result does not apply as it stands to severe obesity. It holds for mostly white, well-off men, and the study received support from Coca-Cola in addition to public funding.

Another cohort, of 9,777 men examined twice about 5 years apart, gives the same kind of signal: those who had moved from “low fitness” to “fit” had a 44% lower risk of death (interval of 25 to 59%) than men who stayed at low fitness.19

Can people really improve? On this point, it is randomised trials that answer. A meta-analysis of 53 trials on high-intensity interval training gives average gains in VO2max, the maximum oxygen the body consumes per minute and per kilo.16

Training improves capacity, including in people with overweight

Average VO2max gain after interval training, by population. Meta-analysis of 53 randomised trials. Source: Wen et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2019.16

What this means

Adults with overweight gain 3.54 mL/kg/min on average: less than healthy adults (5.45), but clearly more than already highly trained athletes (1.71). A high weight does not close the door to progress, and progress is measured by a test, not on the scale.

In his 2021 review, Gaesser concludes that, based on the observational studies gathered, increasing fitness and activity reduces the risk of death more consistently than intentional weight loss. He specifies that only large randomised trials could settle the matter, and that the point is not to oppose weight loss, but not to make it the main criterion.14

All of this rests on observations. Before concluding, we need to examine what could distort them.

Step 6 of 6

What could distort everything, and what remains uncertain

Reverse causation. A person who falls ill loses weight and exercise capacity: both are low because the illness is there, and death follows. Two safeguards exist in the data reviewed: the BMI analysis excludes smokers, people with chronic disease and deaths in the first five years,9 and the study of changes in fitness measures what happens afterwards, over more than ten years.13 They reduce the problem; they do not eliminate it.

Who the people studied are. The large cohorts are largely American, drawn from clinics, with fairly well-off participants and, for the 2025 meta-analysis, 67% men. The Ortega study includes 98% white participants, often white-collar workers.1,7 Data are lacking for Africa, India and China.

What “fit” means. Each study splits its population into groups, and the line varies. In Barry's meta-analysis, “fit” covered roughly the top 75 to 80% for age.4 The contrast is therefore mainly between the lowest quarter or fifth and everyone else. It does not show that you need to aim for the elite.

Weight stands in for composition. In the 2025 meta-analysis, only two studies out of twenty measure fat mass directly: the “overweight” and “obesity” categories rest on BMI, which misses some of the cases of excess fat (step 1).1

No trial on mortality. Nobody has randomly assigned people to “gain fitness” or not, then counted deaths over decades. The fitness gains obtained in trials are real (step 5); their precise effect on lifespan is known only through observations.

What this means

The result that best withstands the objections: at the same weight, people with low fitness die more than others, including thin people. The result that withstands them less well: that fitness fully cancels the risk of obesity, notably for the heart and over the long term.

The answer to the problem

Back to the question: do weight and fitness measure the same thing? No. Weight measures a total mass, without distinguishing what it contains; BMI misses a good share of excess fat, including in people of normal weight, whose metabolic profile may be impaired. Fitness measures the capacity of your heart, lungs and muscles to produce effort. Across 400,000 observations, it is fitness that separates the trajectories at the same weight, with a risk of death about doubled in people with low fitness, thin people included.

When your scale goes down, does your fitness go up? Not necessarily: in the study of changes, what was associated with survival was the change in exercise capacity, not in weight. And when your scale reads low, are you fit? No more so. Camille and Thomas, our starting example, cannot be told apart on the scale.

Level of certainty. Solid: the association between low fitness and increased mortality at all weights, found in different cohorts and methods; the ability of BMI to miss excess fat; the fact that fitness improves with training, including in people with overweight. Probable: that changing your fitness changes the risk, without the size of the effect being known. Not demonstrated: that fitness is enough to cancel the risk of obesity, in particular cardiovascular risk and over long periods, and that weight loss has no benefit. Obesity remains a risk factor; what these studies show is that it does not sum up your health, and neither does thinness.

What to put in place

What follows is a coaching approach deduced from these results, not a protocol proven as such. Where no study reviewed quantifies a practice, this is stated.

  1. Measure two things separately.Keep the scale if it is useful to you, and add the test on the page. These are two questions, two columns. You can have a stable weight and rising fitness, or the opposite.
  2. Track performance, not only weight.Choose the test result as your main reference (time, distance, load, repetitions depending on the page). The step 5 data point this way: the capacity that changes is what is associated with survival.
  3. First, move up from the lowest level.The reviews cited report that the biggest gains come from moving from inactivity to moderate activity, with benchmarks of 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity; these can be split across the day.14
  4. Work on muscle too.Lean mass is associated with survival in older adults (step 2). No study read here quantifies the gain of a strength programme on mortality: this is a choice of coherence, not a proof. The strength tests on this site give you the tracking.
  5. Retest under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. A field test estimates VO2max only with a correlation of 0.66 to 0.84 according to a meta-analysis of 57 studies, and the variation from one run of the Cooper test to the next is about 52 metres in runners: a smaller difference proves nothing.17,18 An interval of 8 to 12 weeks leaves time for progress to exceed this noise; this is a coaching benchmark, and no study read sets this duration.
  6. Keep an eye on your metabolic health.A poor profile (blood pressure, blood glucose, blood fats) is a risk whatever the weight, according to Kramer's meta-analysis.8 If your BMI is 30 or more, or if you have chest pain or abnormal breathlessness, talk to a doctor before increasing your training.
What these figures do not say
  • These are almost all observational studies: they show associations, not causes.
  • The populations are mostly male, American and well-off. Applicability to other groups has not been demonstrated.
  • Weight categories rest on BMI, which does not distinguish fat from muscle.
  • Several results have wide intervals (fit people with obesity, cardiovascular risk, normal-weight women with high fat mass): caution is needed before citing them as established.

Frequently asked questions

So is losing weight pointless?

That is not what these data say. Obesity increases the risk of death (step 4), and a high BMI remains associated with risks that fitness does not always seem to erase, especially for the heart. They show that weight should not be the only indicator, nor the main criterion of success.9,14

I am thin: do I need a fitness test?

Yes, this is precisely the case where the scale reassures wrongly: normal-weight people with low fitness have about twice the risk of those who are fit.1

Should I aim for a specific fat mass?

The studies reviewed give no individual target. They use population thirds (above 23.1% in men and 33.3% in women in the Mayo study), which are not health thresholds.11

Does high fitness mean I can ignore my weight?

Not entirely: for cardiovascular mortality, the excess risk of fit people with overweight or obesity is not ruled out, and it appears over the long term in the longest analyses.1,8
